title: Arjuna drops his bow
hook: Arjuna drops his bow and wants out; Krishna answers with karma yoga
carry: karma yoga: every act can be an offering
tomorrow: a king hears his city is on fire and says nothing of his burns. how?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of the Upanishads. Your line was the silence after om is the fourth.
screen: `THE SILENCE AFTER OM IS THE FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Back to the battlefield. Arjuna, the finest archer of his day, stands in a chariot between two armies, with Krishna at the reins. He looks across and sees his teachers, his uncles, his cousins. His mouth goes dry. His great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and he sits down on the floor of the chariot. Better to live as a beggar, he says, than to do this. It's the oldest kind of wanting out: not this duty, not this family, not this day. Krishna's answer opens the first of Hinduism's three great paths.
screen: `BETWEEN TWO ARMIES.` → `THE BOW SLIPS. HE SITS.` → `BETTER TO BEG THAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: Arjuna even makes a clever argument. Krishna, you said knowing is higher than doing. So why push me into this terrible act? Krishna's answer, in chapter three of the Bhagavad Gita, is the root of karma yoga. Karma means action; yoga means joining. First: nobody gets out of acting. Not for a moment, he says. Even keeping the body alive is action. Sitting down in the chariot is a choice too. So the question isn't whether you'll act, but how. Then the key: the world is bound by action, except action done as yajna, as an offering. Yajna was the old fire sacrifice: something precious poured into the flame and never taken back. Krishna widens it to everything. Later he says it plainly: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me. That's karma yoga. Do the act as well as you can, then let it go into God's hands, like a flower set down at a shrine. It's why many Hindus offer food before eating, and why some close a task with a quiet word: Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna. Hindu teachers draw three great paths from the Gita: karma, the path of action; bhakti, devotion; jnana, knowledge. Arjuna's duty was a warrior's, on a terrible day. Most of us get the dishes and the night shift. The teaching doesn't ask anyone to leave the sink. It changes how you hold what's in your hands.
screen: `KARMA YOGA: THE PATH OF ACTION.` · `NOBODY GETS OUT OF ACTING.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, AS AN OFFERING.` · `KRISHNARPANAM: OFFERED TO KRISHNA.` · then, large: `EVERY ACT CAN BE AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Think of the next ordinary task on your list, and picture doing it carefully, the way you'd prepare something for someone you love. Then picture setting it down like a flower at a shrine and walking away, without looking back to see who noticed. If you pray, finish it silently the way many Hindus do, Krishnarpanam, or offer it to God as you understand God; if not, offer it to the people it will help.
Karma yoga, the path of action as offering. Nobody can stop acting, Krishna tells Arjuna, so offer whatever you do.
Your line: karma yoga: every act can be an offering. Arjuna's bow is still on the chariot floor. See you tomorrow.
